commit_uploads.message:
Ship the licence texts, close the release-pipeline gaps, and fuzz the registry (#89)

The third parity pass. With this the blueprint audit stands at **78/81**, against
52/78 at the start; the three that remain are decisions rather than open work
(branch protection, declined twice; the citation keys, now tied to the release
state by a guard; and a per-binding second test kind).

## Licences

Every manifest declared `MIT OR Apache-2.0`, but an SPDX expression is a
reference to two documents rather than the documents — each published package
went out leaving whoever received it with terms to go and find.

- Committed copies in `wickra-terminal-core`, `ui-tui` and `bindings/python`.
  Cargo decides what to package from git, which narrows the options to one: an
  untracked copy makes `cargo publish` refuse the dirty tree, and an ignored one
  is dropped from the `.crate` entirely. Committed copies drift, which is what
  `check_license_copies.py` now watches — deriving the locations from the
  workspace, so a new publishable crate starts requiring its licences without
  anyone editing a list.
- The npm side needs both halves and neither works alone: `release.yml` stages
  the texts, and every one of the seven `package.json` files names them in
  `files`, without which npm drops them again without a word. A pack dry-run
  proves it.

## Release pipeline

- **The jar never reached the release page.** `java-publish` deployed to Maven
  Central and uploaded nothing, so every language had an artefact there except
  Java — and provenance had nothing to attest for it.
- **`go-mirror` never compiled what it publishes.** The module tree is assembled
  by copying files and rewriting an import path, and was pushed to pkg.go.dev on
  that basis alone. It now builds against the staged Linux library and runs a
  smoke test that constructs a terminal, subscribes, ticks and reads a chart
  frame back.
- **Provenance covers the `.nupkg` and the `.jar`.** Both were published bare
  while the README badge claimed provenance for the release as a whole.

## Drift and fuzzing

- CI compares the committed napi loader with what napi generates. Both files are
  generated and committed so consumers need no toolchain, and nothing compared
  them — napi rewrites them only when somebody rebuilds, and a rebuild is not
  part of committing.
- A fuzz target that reaches the registry: 7,400 generated lines, one
  construction arm per indicator, and no target touched them. `build` must
  refuse bad parameters rather than panic — zero and negative periods, NaN,
  enormous magnitudes — which is exactly what the completeness suite cannot
  reach, because it drives `DEFAULTS`, by definition the parameters that work.
- The pytest advisory is recorded in `osv-scanner.toml` with its assessment, now
  that a workflow actually reads that file.

## Testing

`cargo test --workspace --all-features` passes, `cargo clippy --workspace
--all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` is clean, and both new check
scripts run green locally.

Show the time-machine in every language, and give WASM an example

Every reach had one example, and it was the same one: open a synthetic
source, tick, print a frame. That shows how to drive the core and cannot
show what the core is for. The capability this repository is named around
-- rewind a recording and have the state rebuild itself deterministically
-- appeared in no example at all, so a reader had to find it in the docs
and work out the JSON.

So there are two scenarios now, in all nine reaches, and the second plays
a recorded feed to its end, asks where it stands, rewinds to the second
trade and shows the frame the forward pass had at that point.

Three languages take the scenario as an argument rather than a directory
of its own, and each for its own reason rather than for consistency's
sake. Go allows one main per package. The C# project file carries forty
lines of native-library plumbing that a second copy would let rot. Rust
already had multiple bin targets, so it gets one more.

And examples/wasm/ did not exist -- the browser was the one reach with no
example, because web/ was assumed to be it. web/ is the product; an
example is the shape. This is one HTML file with no build tool, and it
uses a recorded feed rather than a synthetic one on purpose: rewinding in
WebAssembly with no engine behind it is the thing a page cannot fake.

CI checks both scenarios where it ran one, and parses the WASM page's
module script -- which also asserts that the loader path it imports is
the one wasm-pack actually writes.

Correct three ROADMAP claims that had stopped being true

The "Next" section's first item was two claims that could not both hold:
"1 of the 504 in wickra-core are not reachable", and immediately under it
a list of seventeen derivatives-tick, fifteen cross-section, three
trade-quote and eight profile outputs. The number had been corrected at
some point and the sentence beneath it had not, so the paragraph said
both one and forty-three.

What is true is narrower and worth saying plainly: exactly one indicator
has no registry entry, Footprint, because it answers with a list of price
levels the fixed named-field model does not carry -- and the terminal
already renders a footprint from its own state. The profiles and the
alternative bars are not in that count at all; they have surfaces of
their own.

The cross-section and trade-quote families were never blocked on a feed:
the first reads the markets the terminal already tracks and the second
reads a print against the book it arrived on. Only the derivatives family
is, and that is upstream -- so it is now its own item, naming the thing
that has to change and where.

"Panel-local keys" is removed because they exist: the arrow keys scroll
the focused panel. And the release blocker no longer includes missing
credentials; those moved to the organisation. The dependency is what is
left, which is the whole point of that entry.

Start a live market with its history, and let it be a perpetual

Two gaps that both made the live source less than the exchange layer
already offered.

The terminal built every bar from ticks it saw itself. The exchange trait
has carried klines since the start and nothing called it, so Atr(14) on
an hourly timeframe was silent for fourteen hours of wall clock, and the
chart opened empty on a market that has traded since 2017 -- which reads
as a broken feed rather than as a warmup. A fresh subscription now
fetches 200 bars and seeds the chart, the price history and every
bar-derived indicator from them.

The book, the tape and the footprint are deliberately not seeded. A bar
records that trading happened, not the prints it was made of, and
inventing those would put a depth ladder and a tape on screen that no
venue ever published.

A failed backfill is not a failed subscription: the venue may not carry
the interval, the request may time out, the market may be too new to have
a history, and in each of those the right outcome is a terminal that
starts empty rather than one that refuses to open the market.

The conversion between the exchange's Candle and this crate's is where
the duplicate wickra-core costs something -- the exchange pins 0.9 and
this crate builds against 1, so the compiler sees two identical structs
as unrelated types. One function, said out loud, rather than a little
friction everywhere.

And the market was hard-coded to Spot, so a perpetual could not be opened
at all: the whole derivatives side of the catalogue had no market to
watch, before the question of a funding feed arises. Live specs take a
market now, and the shorthand takes it as a third segment. A symbol
carries a slash and never a colon, so a second colon can only be the
market's -- and a word there that is not a market name is reported rather
than folded into the symbol, which is what used to happen and answered a
typo in the market with a message about an unknown symbol.

Funding and open interest still have no live feed, and that is upstream:
wickra-exchange-core defines DerivativesFeed and DerivativesTickBuilder,
no venue implements them, and the Exchange trait exposes no subscription.
FeedDerivatives stays the only path, which is why it exists. Recorded in
SOURCES.md rather than left looking like an oversight here.

Give the time-machine something to rewind

The terminal could seek through a recording and had no way to make one.
Nothing in the repository wrote a session out, and Replay takes the feed
as JSON rather than a path -- so the only way to get a recording was to
already have one, which made the whole feature reachable in tests and
nowhere else.

A config now sets "record" to a capacity and the terminal keeps that many
recent events. Off by default and deliberately a ring: a terminal left
running overnight must not grow without limit, and what a person reaches
for a recorder for is the last few minutes rather than the whole session.

ExportRecording hands the events back in exactly the shape Replay takes,
so the output goes straight back in as a dataset -- which is the property
that makes this a recorder rather than a debug dump. SetRecording turns it
on and off at run time, clearing what is held either way, because a
capacity change that kept the old events would leave a recording that is
part one size and part another.

The core stays filesystem-free, because it has to be to run in a browser,
so it records into memory and the renderer writes. The TUI binds w, goes
through the command boundary rather than serialising the events itself --
so the file is byte-for-byte what any other binding would get -- and names
the file by the wall clock rather than overwriting one path, because what
a person saves is a moment they want to keep.

Events are recorded as they are polled, not as they are folded. fold is
also how a seek re-folds a recording, so recording there would append the
replayed events back onto the recording and every rewind would double it.
There is a test for exactly that.

Stop folding a live market after it is unsubscribed

LiveSource::unsubscribe was a comment explaining that the exchange client
has no per-symbol unsubscribe, and a body that did nothing. The comment
was true and the conclusion did not follow: the fold creates state for
whatever market an event names, so the dropped market arrived on the very
next poll, its state was rebuilt, and it was folded for the rest of the
session -- indicators, book, tape and all -- invisible, because the
watchlist no longer listed it.

The source filters its own output now, which is what the replay, synthetic
and manual sources already did; live was the only one that did not. The
socket is still the venue's to close, and that stays true. The work is
not.

The filter is a free function so it can be tested. Everything either side
of it needs a socket, and this is the part that decides what the terminal
folds -- the part that was wrong.

Let the browser read the keymap it was always given

Keybinds live in the config expressly so both renderers share one: rebind
next_symbol once and the TUI and the browser both move. Only the TUI ever
read it, so that was true of the config and false of the product.

The key names are the TUI's, because the map is shared -- backtab means
Shift+Tab in both, even though crossterm reports it as a key of its own
and the browser reports Tab with a modifier. A key held with Ctrl, Cmd or
Alt is left alone: Ctrl+R is a reload and Cmd+L is the address bar, and a
terminal that stole those would be a worse citizen than one with fewer
shortcuts. So is a key pressed inside a field, or typing ETH/USDT into
the subscribe box would fire the t binding on its way past.

Where the renderers differ they differ in idiom, not meaning: an action
that opens a modal prompt in the TUI focuses the matching field here.
Three do nothing in a browser and report that rather than pretending --
quit, because a tab is not the terminal's to close, and the panel-focus
and scroll pairs, because a web panel is a scrollable box the browser
already drives.

isTyping is duck-typed rather than an instanceof HTMLElement: that name
only exists in a browser, so the check would throw wherever the module is
loaded without one, for a question that has a good answer there.

Make panels as deep as the config asks, and let focus scroll them

Panel focus was drawn and acted on nothing. Tab moved a highlighted
border, no key did anything with it, and the ROADMAP listed the gap
without saying what stood in the way -- which was this: the core sent
twelve book levels and twenty-four tape prints because those numbers were
consts in the panel modules, so there was nothing underneath what a
renderer drew to scroll to. Focus had nothing to act on.

So a PanelSpec now carries an optional depth. One number rather than a
name per panel, because every panel that has a bound has exactly one:
book levels a side, tape prints, footprint levels, chart points and bars,
alternative bars per stream. The watchlist and the profile panel have
none and ignore it. Zero is refused rather than honoured -- a panel
configured to carry nothing renders blank with no error, which reads as a
broken feed rather than as a configuration -- and the value is clamped at
512, past which the state's own rings are the ceiling anyway.

It is the carried depth, not the drawn one, and that distinction is the
point: a renderer draws what fits and scrolls through the rest. The TUI
binds that to the arrow keys on the focused panel, clamped after every
frame because the frame is what says how many rows exist -- a tape that
has printed twice must not be scrollable to row forty because the last
one was. The scroll offset stays renderer state, where the architecture
puts focus: the browser already scrolls its panels and needed nothing.

The chart is the one panel that ignores it. It is a plot rather than a
list of rows, and scrolling a plot means panning its axes -- a different
gesture with a different meaning.

Hold every binding to the re-fold guarantee

The terminal reaches a state two ways. Streaming folds one event per tick
as it arrives; Seek throws the state away and re-folds the whole prefix in
a single batch. ARCHITECTURE.md calls that re-fold the moat -- it is what
makes a rewind deterministic and what lets the browser run the
time-machine with no engine behind it.

The Rust suite proved the core re-folds correctly. Nothing proved that
each binding carries the same bytes out, and that is a separate claim:
nine reaches, each marshalling its own strings across the ABI. So each of
the nine now drives the same scenario -- stream four ticks, and on a
second terminal run the feed out and re-fold the same prefix -- and
asserts the two frames are equal as strings. String equality, not a JSON
comparison: every binding returns the core's compact command output
verbatim, so bytes are the exact check and no language needs a parser for
it.

Each carries a second assertion that the compared frames are not empty
ones. Two empty frames are byte-identical too, and an equality test that
passes on nothing proves nothing.

The C++ test sits under examples/c/ with the C one rather than beside the
C++ README, and bindings/cpp/README.md now says why: the C++ surface is a
header inside the C binding, so its tests link the same library and one
CMake project builds both -- which is also what the repository blueprint
prescribes. Compiling them the way a consumer compiles them is the point.
Record the renderer command surface in the changelog

Bind the five commands neither renderer could reach

AddIndicator, RemoveIndicator, SetTimeframe, ListIndicators and Seek were
carried by the boundary, exercised by every binding's tests, and bound to
nothing in either front-end. The consequence was not subtle: the registry
-- the headline feature, 497 indicators -- could only be configured from a
file, and the time-machine had no control anywhere, in either renderer,
which made a recording nothing more than a slow synthetic feed.

Three things were missing and each is fixed here.

The core had no typed way to do any of it. AddIndicator, RemoveIndicator
and SetTimeframe existed only inside command_json, so a Rust embedder had
to assemble JSON to reach its own registry -- which is a fair part of why
neither renderer ever did. They are methods now, and command_json calls
them, so the config stays in step either way.

The DataSource trait has carried cursor() and event_count() from the
start and nothing read them, so no renderer could show where in a
recording it stood. Terminal::replay_position exposes them, and a
ReplayPosition command carries them across the ABI -- the second command
that answers rather than renders. A source that is not a recording
answers 0/0 rather than an error: a live feed has no recorded length, and
a renderer can ask about whatever is focused without first knowing what
kind of source it is. A command rather than a frame field because the
position belongs to a source, not a panel; in the frame it would sit in
front of every consumer that has no replay at all.

And the renderers had no controls. The TUI binds i, k, t, l and , / . --
through the config keymap, which both renderers share, so a rebinding
moves both. The web renderer gets a second control bar with the same
five, a chip per catalogue match that fills the add field, and a scrubber
that follows the source rather than only the seeks the user makes,
because a replay advances by itself as its events are consumed.

The indicator shorthand is one grammar in both renderers -- Sma 20,
Macd 12 26 9, Beta 20 vs ETH/USDT -- and also accepts the label form the
chart prints, so a name read off the screen types straight back in. vs
splits the reference off before the parameters, because a market has
digits in it.

Feed and FeedDerivatives are deliberately still unbound: they are how a
host pushes its own feed in, so their caller is an embedder rather than a
person at a keyboard. RENDERERS.md now says that rather than leaving the
gap to look like the others.

Give the chart bars, and draw them

The chart panel takes seventy percent of the default layout and drew two
lines: a sparkline of eight block glyphs over the last-trade series, and
a row of indicator text. No axis, no price scale, no bar structure -- on
the headline panel of a trading terminal.

The view-model had nothing better to offer. It carried a list of last
prices, and the candle builder kept only the bar in progress: each closed
bar went to the indicators, which read it and kept their own state, so
nothing retained the bars themselves. So ChartView now carries them, out
of a bounded ring of 256 in the state, along with the bar still forming
-- kept apart from the closed ones because it is the one that will still
change, and a chart that omitted it would show the market frozen at the
last close for a whole bar.

Both fields are omitted from the JSON while empty, so a consumer written
against the earlier shape sees the object it saw before. The tick series
stays, and both renderers fall back to it until the first bar closes,
which at an hourly timeframe is the first hour of a session.

The TUI draws the bars on a braille canvas with a price scale beside
them; the web canvas draws the same bars. Bodies are three strokes rather
than a rectangle because a doji has no height, and a rectangle of no
height draws nothing at all -- the one bar shape a trader most wants to
see.

Indicators stay a numeric readout rather than lines over the candles.
An indicator's series is sampled once per tick and the bars are one per
bar, so they do not share an x-axis: an average drawn on the candle axis
would sit near, but not on, the bar it came from, which reads as a real
reading and is not one. Overlays are still drawn in the fallback, where
the two series do share an axis.

Golden fixtures regenerated; the timeframe scenario pins six closed bars
and a forming one.

Teach the web renderer the two panels it never learned

Profile and Bars were added to the core, given view-models, given TUI
widgets, and never reached the web front-end. PanelKind listed five
kinds, PanelView had five variants, and App.vue had five sections -- so
the core emitted both panels in every frame and findPanel never asked for
them. They vanished with no error anywhere.

ARCHITECTURE.md states that adding a panel to the core makes it appear in
every renderer at once. For those two it was not true, and nothing could
have said so: the golden corpus compares frames, and the frames were
correct; the web suite tests the mappings it has. A panel a renderer has
never heard of has no test to fail.

So the guard reads the core's own PanelKind and holds the web renderer to
it in the three places a panel can be dropped independently -- the kind
union, the view union, and a section in the template. It lives in the
core because that is where the list lives.

The profile histogram scales each distribution against its own peak,
which is the decision the TUI widget already makes: volume traded at a
price and a count of time slots are different units, and one shared scale
flattens the smaller into nothing. The scaling moved into its own module
so it is testable without mounting a component, the same reason ./layout
is one.
